facts.text: The spiny-cheeked honeyeater is large for a honeyeater, reaching 22 to 27 centimeters tall and weighing around 52 grams.
facts.quote: It is large for a honeyeater, ranging from  22 to 27 centimeters (8.7 to 10.6 inches) tall and weighing around 52 grams.

facts.text: The spiny-cheeked honeyeater is sociable and aggressive, and is often seen foraging in large flocks.
facts.quote: The birds are sociable, aggressive, and often observed foraging in large flocks.

facts.text: Its beak is long and straight with a black tip, turning fleshy red or pink towards the chin.
facts.quote: Its beak is long and straight with a black tip and a fleshy red or pink colour towards the chin and up to the gape.

facts.text: Young spiny-cheeked honeyeaters have a characteristic yellow cheek sash that is much less pronounced in adults.
facts.quote: The juvenile bird has a characteristic yellow cheek sash, although this is less pronounced in the adult bird, where predominantly the cheek is white with a grey and/or brown streak under the cheek.

facts.text: Breeding can happen in any month, but 75% of eggs in the eastern range appear between late August and mid-November.
facts.quote: Breeding has been recorded in all months, and eggs have been found from June through to March; however, 75% of the eggs would be found between late August and mid-November in the eastern range of the bird.

facts.text: Its deep cup-shaped nest is woven from grass and spider silk and often lined with soft possum fur, hanging hammock-like between two branches.
facts.quote: The nests are deep and cup-shaped, woven with grass, spider silk, and spider egg-sacs. Often the nest is lined with soft materials, like possum fur or pussy tails.

facts.text: It is nomadic in northern Australia but tends to stay local in the south, and is common across its Australian range.
facts.quote: They are considered a nomadic species; however, this seems to be more so in the northern parts of Australia. In the south, they tend to stay in local areas, and are considered to be resident.

facts.text: Nectar makes up about 38% of its diet, though it also eats insects, small lizards, spiders and larvae.
facts.quote: 38% of their diet is nectar; however, insects, small lizards, spiders, and larvae are also in the diet.

facts.text: It lives in habitats ranging from scattered woodland and open woodlands to sparse and closed shrubland.
facts.quote: Other habitats include scattered woodland, open woodlands, sparse shrubland, and closed shrubland.

facts.text: It is found across most of Australia, but not east of the Great Dividing Range, Tasmania, the far south-west of Western Australia or the northern tropics.
facts.quote: The spiny-cheeked honeyeater can be found in most locations throughout Australia, except east of the Great Dividing Range, Tasmania, the far south-west of Western Australia, and the northern Australian tropics.
